pages.description: H.R.28 would bar federally funded schools from allowing students who were born male — as defined by reproductive biology and genetics — to compete in sports programs designated for women or girls. It would make such participation illegal sex discrimination under Title IX.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.28 would bar schools receiving federal aid from allowing “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1]. It would define sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] It would also allow “males to train or practice” [1] under the safeguards quoted below. At the January 14, 2025 vote, NCAA rules allowed transgender women, who are male under the bill’s definition, to qualify under sport-specific conditions: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2] Its May 2024 rules set hormone limits: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [3]

points.title: It protects female athletes’ access to team projects that remove pollution and improve waste practices.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It protects female athletes’ access to team projects that remove pollution and improve waste practices.

  • Because The bill would allow males to practice with female teams only if “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1].
  • Because Team membership provides an organized way to remove pollution. Fordham rower Caitlin Boyle reported: “In the cleanup, 50 of my teammates on Fordham Rowing assisted me with picking up trash along the shores and streets of City Island in bags and then disposing of the waste properly.” [4]
  • Because Those projects also spread knowledge: “Additionally, I held a presentation for the team educating them on basic environmental knowledge and the importance of proper waste management.” [4]
  • Because Teammates help launch wider efforts. Wisconsin rower Grace Latz said: “I started all of this because my teammates were taking similar classes to me and shared the same values, so it made it easier.” [5]
  • Because The recycling group Latz helped start reached other institutions: “Since then, REthink has expanded beyond the UW athletic department to work with the UW campus, the hospital, the Wisconsin unions, dining services and UW housing.” [5]
  • So Protecting female athletes’ places on teams that do this work protects their access to cleanup, environmental teaching and wider recycling campaigns. Preserving these ways to defend nature gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Boyle organized her City Island cleanup in partnership with the New York Department of Sanitation. REthink grew to about 60 members and worked with campus units beyond athletics. Sources: [4], [5].

Evidence note: At the comparison date the NCAA regulated transgender participation sport by sport, with a U.S. Rowing testosterone threshold listed for rowing. Rep. Bonamici told the House that about 10 of roughly 510,000 NCAA athletes were transgender. Sources: [2], [3], [6].

points.title: It protects female rowers’ time on the water, where seeing environmental harm prompts care and action.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects female rowers’ time on the water, where seeing environmental harm prompts care and action.

  • Because The bill’s safeguard for male practice also protects a female athlete’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • Because Rowing gives athletes firsthand knowledge of the waters they use. Wisconsin rower Alexandra Bogner said: “I’ve rowed on both Lake Mendota and Lake Monona and have been able to see the ecological challenges that they face” [7].
  • Because Seeing litter while rowing helped prompt Boyle’s research on school waste management: “Rowing on Long Island further inspired this thesis due to the plethora of trash that is floating around in the ocean.” [4]
  • Because Practice also gave Boyle chances to act: “For the past four years, I have tried to grab every piece of waste out of the ocean at practice that I can reach.” [4]
  • So Protecting female rowers against losing practice time keeps open a route from seeing pollution to removing litter and studying ways to reduce waste. That serves [NAME]’s wish to care for nature and protect it from pollution.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: At the comparison date the NCAA regulated transgender participation sport by sport, with a U.S. Rowing testosterone threshold listed for rowing. Rep. Bonamici told the House that about 10 of roughly 510,000 NCAA athletes were transgender. Sources: [2], [3], [6].

points.title: It protects female athletes’ access to scholarship support for environmental study.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects female athletes’ access to scholarship support for environmental study.

  • Because The bill would allow males to train or practice only if no female lost a “scholarship” [1].
  • Because Athletic aid supports students doing environmental work. Notre Dame described rower Anna Kottkamp as “an environmental science major” [8] who “went on to earn a full athletic scholarship.” [8]
  • Because Kottkamp was “an undergraduate research assistant for Jennifer Tank” [8], studying “the impact of cover crops on agricultural streams.” [8]
  • Because Tank’s research tests ways to protect water from pollution: “Her research combines the wide-scale planting of cover crops in winter with innovative drainage strategies that can reduce fertilizer runoff to streams and rivers.” [9]
  • So Protecting athletic aid for female students doing this work protects financial support for learning how to prevent water pollution. Supporting that way to protect nature gives [NAME] a further reason to favor the bill.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Kottkamp began as a walk-on without previous competitive rowing experience and later earned a full athletic scholarship. Her environmental education curriculum work took place during a 2013 Peru internship supported by a Kellogg Institute fellowship. Sources: [8].

Evidence note: At the comparison date the NCAA regulated transgender participation sport by sport, with a U.S. Rowing testosterone threshold listed for rowing. Rep. Bonamici told the House that about 10 of roughly 510,000 NCAA athletes were transgender. Sources: [2], [3], [6].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect At schools receiving federal aid, H.R.28 would prohibit allowing “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1]. It would define sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]. This would bar otherwise eligible transgender girls and women from competition in those programs. College sailing shows the change from the rules in force on January 14, 2025: its adopted policy stated “For competitions classified as Women’s events, all female-identifying and non-binary sailors are eligible to compete” [10], and its fall 2024 rules retained “Women’s events: Woman or non-binary” [11].

points.title: It removes women’s outdoor competition as a way to develop care for nature.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes women’s outdoor competition as a way to develop care for nature.

  • Because Women’s school teams compete in natural places. At a Malden River cleanup involving Tufts’ women’s rowing team, an athletics coordinator explained that “our rowing athletes train and compete on it almost every day.” [12]
  • Because On the comparison date, NCAA rules could admit transgender women to women’s teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2]
  • Because Outdoor activities can strengthen concern for the environment. In a study of teenagers at a 15-day outdoor camp, “Pairwise comparisons for affective beliefs revealed that scores for the experimental group increased after the intervention (p < .01), whereas scores for the control group underwent no significant change.” [13]
  • Because College sailing gives a concrete example of this link. Harvard describes a sailor’s drive to protect the environment: “It's that time in the water with her teammates that has driven Hogan-Lopez to learn more about the environment and how to protect it.” [14]
  • So The ban would remove women’s outdoor competition from the opportunities available to otherwise eligible transgender students. It would cut off competition’s time in nature and shared experiences as a way to build that care.
  • Note The exception allowing students to “train or practice” [1] does not restore access to competition.
  • So [NAME]’s concern for nature gives [NAME] a reason to preserve this way of developing care for it, and therefore to oppose the bill.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The camp study measured a 15-day programme with about 6-10 hours of activity daily, including trekking, biking, climbing and canoeing. It did not measure school racing. Sources: [13].

Evidence note: College sailing rules for fall 2024 listed open events for all genders, men's events for men or non-binary sailors, and women's events for women or non-binary sailors. H.R.28 restricts programs designated for women or girls, so open events remain, and it allows practice under stated conditions. Harvard's feature credits time on the water with teammates and does not separate racing from practice. Sources: [11], [15], [14].

points.title: It restricts posts for leading environmental work within women’s teams.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It restricts posts for leading environmental work within women’s teams.

  • Because Yale places environmental leaders within individual teams: “each participating varsity and club team has a sustainability captain. That person leads the efforts within their team and tailors the certification program to the schedule and structure of their team.” [16]
  • Because These posts include a “sustainability captain of the varsity women’s swimming and diving team” [16]. That captain described practical care for nature: “We volunteered together at a New Haven Land Trust garden last year and performed manual labor to prepare for spring planting.” [16]
  • Because On the comparison date, NCAA rules could admit transgender women to such teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2]
  • Because Team service also removes pollution and prompts sign-ups for further conservation work. At the Tufts cleanup, “Participants collected 33 bags of trash, which included 16 bags of sorted single use plastic bottles (over 1500 bottles)!” [17] and “many students signed up to continue to be involved with the Friends of the Malden River.” [17]
  • So A post for leading a women’s team’s environmental work is an opportunity tied to participation in that team and a way to bring teammates into practical care for nature.
  • Because The bill expressly reaches “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Note Its exception lets students “train or practice” [1]; it does not preserve a separate environmental leadership post within a women’s program.
  • So The bill would restrict access to these posts for otherwise eligible students it excludes from women’s programs. That cuts off a way for those students to organize practical care for nature.
  • So [NAME] values taking part in defending nature. Keeping these opportunities to lead environmental work open gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose the bill.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Tufts cleanup included about 20 athletes from men's and women's rowing and women's track and field, plus community volunteers. Sources: [17].

pages.bill_title: the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025
statements: that the weak and vulnerable in society be protected
that every person in the world have equal opportunities in life
that everyone be treated justly, even people they don't know
pages.description: H.R.28 would bar federally funded schools from allowing students who were born male — as defined by reproductive biology and genetics — to compete in sports programs designated for women or girls. It would make such participation illegal sex discrimination under Title IX.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on January 14, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect At schools receiving federal funds, H.R.28 would make it unlawful “to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It defines sex by birth: “sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] Male and female below follow this rule.

  • Because By January 14, 2025, the 2024 federal rule had already been struck down; that day's debate acknowledged “last week's court order striking down the regulation” [2].
  • Because The existing federal sports rule allowed separate teams: “a recipient may operate or sponsor separate teams for members of each sex where selection for such teams is based upon competitive skill or the activity involved is a contact sport.” [3]
  • Because College rules still allowed transgender women to compete under hormone-based eligibility rules. The NCAA's May 2024 policy said: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [4]
  • Because H.R.28 writes its restriction into the law itself, which “is amended by adding at the end the following” [1].
  • So H.R.28 would add an express federal birth-sex rule where existing policies allowed this participation. Covered schools would share the same rule, and an agency could not reverse it simply by changing its regulations.

points.title: It protects women's fair chance to earn sporting wins and recognition.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It protects women's fair chance to earn sporting wins and recognition.

  • Because Male puberty builds strength: “increases in testosterone due to puberty promote muscular strength” [5].
  • Because A review of 24 studies of transgender women who were not athletes found that, after 12–36 months of hormone treatment, they likely retained a strength advantage over women who were not transgender: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5]
  • Because Strength matters in speed and power events: “In sports demanding speed and power, muscular strength and the ability to generate high rates of force are recognised as key determinant in athletic success.” [5]
  • So In strength-dependent events, the bill would keep retained male-puberty strength advantages out of the female category. Giving women a meaningful chance to earn sporting rewards serves [NAME]'s concern for equal opportunity and just treatment.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s evidence does not settle whether trained transgender women keep the advantage in speed and power events that its fairness claim needs.

  • Because Its review leaves the effects of hormone treatment in trained people unresolved: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [5]
  • Because The review does not report whether the compared groups had similar training: “The levels of physical activity of the transwomen compared with cisgender women in the studies were not reported.” [5] Here, cisgender women means women who are not transgender.
  • Because A 2024 cross-sectional study of athletes found mixed results. Compared with cisgender women athletes, transgender women athletes had “higher absolute handgrip strength” [6] but “lower relative jump height” [6].
  • So Strength retained by non-athletes does not establish an advantage in a speed or power event among trained athletes, and the one athlete study points in both directions. The authors say that study is not sufficient to guide policy. This response does not show that no advantage exists, and it does not address settings without hormone limits.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. CRS reports that some states and school districts allowed participation with no particular requirements or restrictions. Sources: [4], [7].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It protects girls' places in sport and their chances to gain education, health, and leadership benefits.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects girls' places in sport and their chances to gain education, health, and leadership benefits.

  • Because Former college swimmer Paula Scanlan testified to actual lost places: “I know women who have lost roster spots and spots on the podium.” [10]
  • Because The bill allows male training or practice only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where places or sports aid are limited, the competition ban and the practice condition protect female athletes from losing them to male participants. For a girl who needs sports aid to attend college, protecting that aid preserves a route into education.
  • Because Girls in positive sports programs report better mental health. A 2024 study found: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because A 2024 survey of U.S. adults who had played girls' or women's sports found reported gains in leadership skills: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So Keeping a girl's place in a good program preserves her chance to gain these benefits. Protecting routes into education, well-being, and adult leadership serves [NAME]'s concern for equal opportunities in life.
points.con_html:
Response The place-protection reason depends on the fairness claim in reason 1; it does not independently show that reserving places advances equal opportunity.

  • Because The bill's practice exception requires that “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where a place is limited, the bill decides which student holds it. That shows who keeps the benefit, not that the allocation is fairer.
  • Because The mental-health finding concerns access to a good program: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because The leadership finding concerns benefits attributed to participation: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So These benefits follow whoever holds the place, so they do not resolve who has a fair claim to it. This reason adds to [NAME]’s equal-opportunity concern only so far as the fairness claim in reason 1 holds. This response does not dispute that some female athletes would keep places and their benefits under the bill.

points.title: It protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and the lost games that safety concerns can cause.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and the lost games that safety concerns can cause.

  • Because World Rugby links contact-sport risk to “the size, force- and power-producing advantages conferred by testosterone during puberty and adolescence, and the resultant player welfare risks this creates” [13].
  • Because Its review explains the danger to a smaller player: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.” [13]
  • Because World Rugby's review of 12 months of testosterone suppression concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.” [13]
  • So In school contact competition such as rugby, excluding male competitors who have gone through male puberty removes this source of size and force mismatch. That protects athletes who are less able to withstand those forces.
  • Because Safety concerns have also cost whole teams games. After Payton McNabb's 2022 volleyball injury, her school board voted “to forfeit the remaining varsity and junior varsity volleyball games against Highlands School” [14], which the report describes as “attended by the transgender player.” [14] The report states: “The board cited safety concerns for players.” [14] That player's status is unconfirmed: “It is not possible to verify this athlete was trans.” [15]
  • So Where covered competition would otherwise include male competitors, the bill also removes that reason for a school to withdraw its girls' team. Protecting athletes from added collision risks and removing that ground for forfeits serves [NAME]'s concern for the weak and vulnerable, including girls [NAME] does not know.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: World Rugby's October 2020 summary states that there were no direct studies on trans women rugby players. Its collision estimate models typical male mass against typical female mass. The review cited by the PRO says hormone-naive transgender women may not on average have the same athletic attributes as cisgender men. Sources: [16], [13], [5].

Evidence note: The McNabb injury occurred on September 1, 2022. North Carolina's state ban took effect August 16, 2023 and applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [14], [17].

Evidence note: Snopes (March 2025) states that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender, and that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. It reports that the school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence, that the board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players while several coaches spoke for continuing, and that North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, with their sports unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [15], [2], [18].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.28 would require federally funded schools and colleges to exclude transgender girls and women from competition in girls’ and women’s sports under Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education. It bars permitting “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1] and determines sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] This would end participation already allowed under some rules: the NCAA’s May 2024 policy said, “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [19]

points.title: It takes away a route to learning and educational opportunities that other students keep.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It takes away a route to learning and educational opportunities that other students keep.

  • Because Sports teach useful skills: “Sports provide meaningful opportunities for kids to feel confident in themselves and learn valuable life lessons about teamwork, leadership, and communication.” [2]
  • Because Team participation also brings educational openings. The bill itself names “scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • Because The ban reaches beyond matches to “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because The same birth-based rule also restricts nonbinary students it classifies as male. Nonbinary students do not identify only as girls or boys. The Equality Caucus explains: “It would also limit the ability of non-binary and intersex students to participate in these programs as well.” [20]
  • Because Girls born with variations in sex traits also face uncertain eligibility. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [2]. They describe the resulting barrier: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [2]
  • So Blocking team competition and the activities tied to it takes away chances to learn and advance. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities includes transgender, nonbinary, and intersex students, giving a reason to oppose these barriers.
  • Note Permission for “males to train or practice” [1] restores neither eligibility to compete nor equal access to team places and benefits. Even practice is conditional: it is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1], among other protected opportunities.
points.con_html:
Response For students past male puberty, listing the benefits of a lost team place does not show that the eligibility rule denies equal opportunity.

  • Because Fair opportunity can require limits on entry to a sports category. In Clark, a court upheld excluding boys from girls’ volleyball because “due to average physiological differences, males would displace females to a substantial extent if they were allowed to compete for positions on the volleyball team.” [21] The reason was a real difference affecting fair competition, rather than the mere existence of separate teams.
  • Because Previous eligibility under a testosterone limit does not establish equal competitive conditions. Reviewing physical traits after male puberty, Hilton and Lundberg reported that “the muscular advantage enjoyed by transgender women is only minimally reduced when testosterone is suppressed.” [22]
  • So Equal opportunity requires a fair basis for eligibility, not preservation of every existing route to scholarships, learning, or admission. For these students, the PRO must show why the boundary unfairly blocks comparable students; naming benefits and affected identities does not supply that step. This response does not reach students who have not gone through male puberty, sports where no advantage has been shown, or eligible girls deterred by uncertainty about intersex variations.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. CRS reports that some states and school districts allowed participation with no particular requirements or restrictions. Sources: [4], [7].

points.title: It replaces individual protection against unfair treatment with automatic exclusion.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It replaces individual protection against unfair treatment with automatic exclusion.

  • Because The rule makes no distinction by age or sport: “this bill is a blanket ban that treats every age student in every sport the same.” [2]
  • Because On the comparison date, Fourth Circuit law protected an individual girl’s participation, while nationally “Courts have reached different conclusions” [7]. In its April 2024 B.P.J. decision, the Fourth Circuit noted that puberty-blocking treatment meant “B.P.J. has never experienced elevated levels of circulating testosterone.” [23]
  • Because The court held that applying West Virginia’s ban would “treat her worse than people to whom she is similarly situated, deprive her of any meaningful athletic opportunities, and do so on the basis of sex.” [23]
  • So H.R.28 would make birth sex decisive even in cases where a court had held, under the law then in force, that exclusion treated an individual girl worse than comparable students. Replacing that Title IX protection with a duty to exclude conflicts with treating everyone justly. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: B.P.J.'s court found a genuine dispute of material fact on competitive advantage and left her equal-protection claim for further proceedings. In September 2024 the Ninth Circuit upheld a preliminary order on equal-protection grounds in Doe v. Horne. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in B.P.J. and Hecox on July 3, 2025, after the comparison date. On June 30, 2026 the Supreme Court reversed the B.P.J. and Hecox judgments (see note LAW-01). Sources: [23], [24], [7], [25].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [26].

points.title: It removes support and adds stigma for students already facing serious distress and isolation.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It removes support and adds stigma for students already facing serious distress and isolation.

  • Because CDC’s national 2023 high school survey found greater distress and less belonging among transgender students and those unsure whether they were transgender than among peers whose gender matched their sex assigned at birth: “Transgender and questioning students experienced a higher prevalence of violence, poor mental health, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and unstable housing, and a lower prevalence of school connectedness than their cisgender peers.” [27]
  • Because School sports offer health and belonging: “Sports participation is linked to increased academic achievement and fosters in students increased emotional, mental, and physical well-being and a sense of community.” [2]
  • Because Denying team membership also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference describes that exclusion as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [2]
  • So Taking away this source of support while adding stigma burdens students who already need protection. [NAME]’s concern for vulnerable people gives a reason to oppose that harm.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The CDC figures come from a cross-sectional school survey and do not compare outcomes under different sports eligibility rules. The bill permits practice under its stated conditions. Sources: [27], [1].

points.title: It removes a safe way for some girls to compete.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It removes a safe way for some girls to compete.

  • Because A boys’ team is not a safe substitute for every excluded girl. In B.P.J.’s case, the court explained: “By participating on boys teams, B.P.J. would be sharing the field with boys who are larger, stronger, and faster than her because of the elevated levels of circulating testosterone she lacks.” [23]
  • Because The court identified the resulting risk: “It also would expose B.P.J. to the same risk of unfair competition—and, in some sports, physical danger—from which the defendants claim to be shielding cisgender girls.” [23]
  • So H.R.28 removes girls’ team eligibility even in these circumstances. For girls seeking to keep competing on a sex-separated school team, the alternative brings this added danger. Protecting vulnerable students gives [NAME] a reason to oppose shifting that risk onto them.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: B.P.J.'s dispute concerned girls' cross country and track teams. The court referred to physical danger "in some sports". Sources: [23].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [26].

points.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity, and bodily safety at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity, and bodily safety at risk.

  • Because Schools must apply the rule without a set verification process. Representative Hayes notes: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [28]
  • Because A comparable Florida ban led to inquiries into a child’s private history. AP reported: “They interviewed officials at Monarch and at the daughter's middle and elementary schools, seeking to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29]
  • Because The inquiry also reached teammates’ knowledge of her body: “When investigators interviewed the Monarch volleyball players, they said the team did not change clothes or shower together, so they were never disrobed with Norton's daughter.” [29]
  • Because The inquiry was followed by the girl’s withdrawal from school. AP reported, “That all ended when the investigation began and the girl left Monarch.” [29] It added, “The girl now attends school online.” [29]
  • Because Women’s rights organizations warn that sex verification may involve “forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2]. They identify a further danger from such procedures: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2].
  • So A nationwide duty to enforce birth-sex eligibility creates grounds for the same kind of intrusive inquiries, with risks of exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling, and, as those organizations warn, abuse. Protecting children from these harms gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule.
  • Note The supporter’s reply, “There is no requirement for inspections” [2], does not answer the risk. The documented records checks and interviews already invaded privacy. An exam mandate is not needed for that harm.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s evidence does not establish that the bill would lead to bodily examinations or resulting sexual abuse.

  • Because H.R.28 restricts participation in programs “designated for women or girls.” [1] Its text adds no requirement for bodily examinations.
  • Because AP describes an inquiry into records and knowledge: investigators sought “to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29] That account reports no bodily examination.
  • Because Florida’s birth-sex law provides a records-based way to decide eligibility: a birth certificate is accepted if its sex statement “was filed at or near the time of the student's birth.” [30]
  • So The step to bodily examinations and sexual abuse rests on an organizational warning, not on a documented case in the PRO’s evidence. This response does not answer the PRO’s documented privacy harms from records checks and interviews, or the disrupted schooling that followed.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The Florida inquiry also examined staff handling of records, and the student's mother faced discipline. NCAA policy already required annual eligibility documentation from transgender women athletes. FERPA regulations limit officials' access to records in which they have legitimate educational interests. Sources: [29], [19], [31].

Evidence note: Idaho's statute included a separate sex-dispute verification process, which the Ninth Circuit described as allowing gynecological exams. The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [32], [1].

points.title: It exposes students to appearance-based accusations and unequal burdens from enforcing the rule.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It exposes students to appearance-based accusations and unequal burdens from enforcing the rule.

  • Because Enforcing birth-sex eligibility invites suspicion of girls who do not fit stereotypes. Women’s rights organizations warn that verification practices “are especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity, other women and girls who do not conform to sexist stereotypes, and nonbinary and gender nonconforming students.” [2]
  • Because Such accusations have harmed girls who are not transgender. Describing a Utah basketball player targeted for short hair and baggy clothes, the same letter reports: “As a result, the student was subjected to harassment, bullying, and threats of violence, necessitating police protection for her and her family.” [2]
  • Because Utah’s school board independently confirmed harm from the public accusation, recording “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” [33]. Public accusations themselves expose children to abuse.
  • So Extending this eligibility rule nationwide exposes students to harassment for their appearance and, as those organizations warn, unequal scrutiny tied to race and gender stereotypes. That conflicts with treating everyone justly and protecting vulnerable children.
  • So Facing accusations, threats, or humiliating checks also creates a barrier to playing for girls who remain eligible. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities supplies a further reason to oppose this effect of enforcing the rule.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A court had blocked Utah's categorical ban before the February 2024 episode. Utah's fallback commission was then deciding transgender girls' eligibility. The official censure attributed the harm to the board member's public post and comments. Sources: [34], [35], [33].

points.title: It puts educational aid serving other students at risk when schools retain inclusive teams.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It puts educational aid serving other students at risk when schools retain inclusive teams.

  • Because The bill makes inclusion a new Title IX violation: “It shall be a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] to permit the participation it bars.
  • Because Existing enforcement law allows “the termination of or refusal to grant or to continue assistance under such program or activity” [36] after an “express finding on the record, after opportunity for hearing, of a failure to comply with such requirement” [36]. It also requires a finding “that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means.” [36]
  • Because That aid supports education beyond the individual athlete. CRS explains: “The Department of Education (ED) distributes substantial funding to elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions” [7].
  • So Schools that keep including these students would put aid for the affected program at risk, exposing other students to losses too. [NAME]’s concern for students’ equal opportunities gives a reason to oppose making inclusion grounds for withdrawing that support.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Section 1682 requires a hearing, an express finding and a failed attempt at voluntary compliance, and limits termination to the particular program. In 2025 a court restrained a USDA freeze of Maine funds on procedural grounds and the parties settled; Maine and California refused to change their policies and DOJ sued. Sources: [36], [7].

pages.bill_title: the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025
statements: to be tolerant toward all kinds of people and groups
to listen to and understand people who are different to them
to accept people even when they disagree with them
pages.description: H.R.28 would bar federally funded schools from allowing students who were born male — as defined by reproductive biology and genetics — to compete in sports programs designated for women or girls. It would make such participation illegal sex discrimination under Title IX.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on January 14, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.28 would make it a Title IX violation for education programs receiving federal aid to allow “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] This would change eligibility where gender identity governed access: California law required school sports participation “consistent with his or her gender identity, irrespective of the gender listed on the pupil’s records.” [2] The 2024 federal rule had already been struck down by January 14, 2025; reporting on that ruling noted: “The now-vacated Title IX rule did not directly address athletics” [3].

points.title: The bill removes a barrier to participation for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes who are male under its definition.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes a barrier to participation for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes who are male under its definition.

  • Because Such an objection has led a team to give up a game: “A Vermont Christian high school forfeited a girls basketball game because the opposing team had a transgender player, the head of school said.” [4]
  • Because The school's complaint explains the religious basis of its objection: “sex is immutable.” [5] It says competing in that matchup would affirm the opposite, “in violation of its beliefs.” [5]
  • So In covered girls' competitions, the bill removes the matchup that triggers this objection. Girls with that conviction can compete without giving it up.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement includes accepting girls whose religious or other beliefs differ from [NAME]'s. Keeping a way for them to play puts that acceptance into practice.
  • So [NAME] has a reason grounded in tolerance to favor removing this cost of disagreement.
  • Note Acceptance also has room for cooperation across the competition boundary. The bill allows “males to train or practice with an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1] if no female loses a place, opportunity, scholarship, admission, or other sports benefit. Shared training remains a way to work together across differences.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO confuses accepting girls who object to a matchup with accepting their rule for who else may compete.

  • Because The complaint explains the school's religious objection to playing the matchup: “it would be affirming that sex is mutable, in violation of its beliefs.” [5] That explains the objection; it does not make meeting the school's demand an act of accepting people across differences.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement does not mean adopting their demands about others. UNESCO's declaration on tolerance makes the distinction explicit: “It means that one is free to adhere to one's own convictions and accepts that others adhere to theirs.” [6]
  • Because H.R.28 would make it unlawful for federally funded programs to allow “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It would apply the same rule across covered programs, whether anyone objects or not. Its definition rests on “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]
  • So The forfeit explains why the school wants a different rule for who may compete. It does not show why respecting these girls gives [NAME] a reason based on tolerance to impose that rule on other participants.
  • Because The training exception begins, “Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to prohibit” [1]. It leaves shared training possible under stated conditions; it requires no cooperation across differences.
  • So Permission to train together does not supply the missing link between enforcing the objection and accepting people despite disagreement.

points.title: Protecting girls' team places preserves opportunities to practise understanding and acceptance.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Protecting girls' team places preserves opportunities to practise understanding and acceptance.

  • Because The competition rule prevents male competitors from taking female roster places. Even shared training is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1], among other protected benefits.
  • Because Girls' teams can offer a setting for learning to work with different people. A player in a study of two multiethnic high school teams described her own learning: “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” [7]
  • So Protecting girls against this loss of places and practice access preserves their access to those shared learning experiences.
  • So [NAME]'s wish for people to listen to, understand, and accept others gives a reason to protect girls' opportunities to practise those habits with teammates.
points.con_html:
Response The cited study does not establish that the team places protected by the bill offer practice in accepting different people.

  • Because The change the study reports from team play is that it “made players more collectivistic in response to a values questionnaire.” [7] The questionnaire's example of that outlook was “I agree with Emily, learning to play as a team is more important.” [7] That measures the weight given to team goals, a different outcome from acceptance of people with different beliefs. It neither shows nor rules out such acceptance.
  • Because The player's statement, “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” [7], appears in an account of what she learned about group dynamics. In the same passage she complains about team cohesion and says, “I think we need team bonding.” [7]
  • So The link from a team place to practice in accepting different people rests on one player’s unelaborated use of the word tolerance, in a passage about team cohesion. This response does not dispute that she names tolerance as something she learned, or that the teams were multiethnic.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The girls' basketball study reports that its workshops, a three-session intervention, did not have the intended effect of increasing understanding of a different value system. That result concerns the intervention, not team play. The study's measured seasonal change was toward collectivistic responses; it did not measure acceptance of others. It covered two Los Angeles-area teams. Sources: [7].

points.title: The required study makes girls' experiences part of the evidence lawmakers must receive.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The required study makes girls' experiences part of the evidence lawmakers must receive.

  • Because The bill orders Congress's audit office to document “adverse psychological, developmental, participatory, and sociological results to girls” [1] from male participation, including “displacement or discouragement from sports participation” [1].
  • Because This inquiry concerns the benefits protected by the shared-training rule. It studies “benefits to women or girls of participating in single sex sports that would be lost by allowing males to participate.” [1]
  • Because The findings must reach the House and Senate education committees in “a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So The bill requires official examination of these experiences and delivery of the findings to lawmakers. [NAME]'s wish to understand people with different experiences gives a reason to favor this duty to investigate and report.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The report mandate is directed to listed adverse consequences for girls and the meaning of benefits protected by the practice exception. It does not require a balanced inquiry into all experiences of shared sport. That limits the report's scope; it does not remove the PRO's narrower information route. Sources: [1].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.28 would require schools receiving federal money to exclude students it classifies as male from girls’ and women’s sports competition. It makes it unlawful “to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It decides sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] This would bar transgender girls and women and nonbinary students whom the bill classifies as male from those competitions.

points.title: It replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.

  • Because As of January 14, 2025, Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, protected participation in at least some cases. In a 2024 case, “The Fourth Circuit ruled that application of the West Virginia law to the plaintiff violated Title IX, because it treated her worse than those similarly situated based on her sex and caused her harm.” [8]
  • Because Individual differences mattered to that ruling. The court criticized a ban that applied “regardless of whether a particular student has any genuine athletic advantages” [8]. H.R.28 would instead make birth biology and genetics decisive for every student it classifies as male.
  • Because [NAME] values accepting people even when they disagree. That gives weight to including a classmate despite disagreement about that classmate’s gender, and to hearing the student’s circumstances before ruling them out.
  • So The bill would close a route to acceptance that the law then in force protected. Hearing individual students or choosing inclusion as a school community could no longer change eligibility under its birth-based rule.
  • Because The restriction also reaches activities tied to team membership. The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Shared sports offer chances to know people. Researchers describe “regular social interaction; opportunities to build positive relationships with teammates and coaches” [9].
  • Because Exclusion also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that “denying transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth the chance to participate only serves to deny them an opportunity to be part of that community, further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10]
  • Note The limited permission for “males to train or practice” [1] does not restore eligibility to compete on girls’ and women’s teams.
  • So Required exclusion takes away shared competition and team-linked opportunities to build understanding, while reinforcing stigma against these classmates. [NAME]’s wish to accept and understand different people gives a reason to preserve those opportunities and resist that treatment.
points.con_html:
Response Accepting a person does not require agreeing on team eligibility, so losing eligibility is not by itself a loss of acceptance.

  • Because Accepting people across disagreements leaves room to disagree about rules. [NAME] can listen to a student, understand their circumstances, and accept them while reaching a different view about team eligibility. The research defining this value says it concerns “accepting and understanding those with life-styles and beliefs different from one’s own.” [11]
  • Because The bill sets a rule for sports eligibility: “For the purposes of this subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] A decision under that rule does not establish how classmates regard or listen to the student.
  • So Treating eligibility itself as acceptance assumes the point at issue. This response does not answer the PRO’s claims that exclusion reduces contact and team-linked chances to build understanding, adds stigma, or removes a school’s choice to include.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The cited study compared any sports team participation with none. It did not compare acceptance with and without access to girls' competition. The bill allows conditional training or practice. Sources: [9], [1].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [12].

points.title: Its unclear birth-based test puts girls with intersex traits at risk of exclusion.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Its unclear birth-based test puts girls with intersex traits at risk of exclusion.

  • Because Intersex variations are differences in sex traits. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [10].
  • Because These groups report exclusion under comparable rules: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [10]
  • Because Accepting all kinds of people includes accepting people born with different bodies. Their sex traits give [NAME] a reason to make room for them in shared school life.
  • So Exposing these girls to exclusion because their bodies do not fit a simple birth-based test conflicts with that acceptance. [NAME] has a reason to oppose this risk.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The letter names no specific ban or exclusion and gives no worked example of how conflicting traits would be treated. During debate the bill manager said the bill "deals with men in sports" when asked about intersex children. Sources: [10], [10].

points.title: It gives sex-based accusations more power to threaten girls’ places on teams.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It gives sex-based accusations more power to threaten girls’ places on teams.

  • Because Schools would have to follow a rule making birth sex decisive. The bill applies to “a recipient of Federal financial assistance who operates, sponsors, or facilitates athletic programs or activities” [1].
  • So Where schools have included transgender girls, the bill would make a claim that a girl was born male grounds to challenge her eligibility. This gives such accusations a route to exclusion.
  • Because That route has already operated under Utah’s school sports eligibility rules. Associated Press reported that Utah’s athletics association “secretly investigated a female athlete — without telling her or her parents — after receiving complaints from the parents of two girls she had defeated in competition questioning whether the girl was transgender.” [13] The complaint was “among several the association had looked into in its efforts to comply with the Utah law” [13].
  • Because Public accusations can also bring harassment. In a separate 2024 case, Utah’s education board found that a member’s post insinuated “that one of the female students in the picture may not be female” [14]. It recorded “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” [14] resulting from the post and comments.
  • Because Girls who look different face a particular risk. The women’s rights and sports groups warn that sex checks are “especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity” [10].
  • Note The bill’s manager says, “There is no requirement for inspections” [10]. Sex challenges and public accusations do not require physical exams.
  • So The bill creates grounds for exclusion that can turn differences in bodies, appearance, and gender expression into sources of suspicion and harassment. [NAME]’s tolerance toward different people gives a reason to oppose that risk, including, as those groups warn, an added risk for girls of color.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Salt Lake Tribune dates the Utah complaint to the year before the ban took effect in July 2022, when the association let registered transgender athletes compete after a year of hormone blockers. An association spokesman said many parents raised such complaints and none was verified. The state had one registered transgender female athlete on a girls' team that year. AP separately reported that the complaint was among several examined in efforts to comply with the law. Sources: [15], [13].
