directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect If effective on January 14, 2025, H.R.28 would reserve female competition in federally funded athletics for people female at birth: it forbids recipients “to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1]

  • Because The bill defines sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]
  • Because On the vote date, NCAA eligibility still followed sport-specific rules: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [2]
  • Because Shared practice remains allowed under a condition: “The bill does not prohibit male individuals from training or practicing with programs or activities for women or girls as long as such training or practice does not deprive any female of corresponding opportunities or benefits.” [3]

points.title: It removes a source of serious injury risk in female contact sports.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes a source of serious injury risk in female contact sports.

  • Because Hormone-based eligibility allowed these matchups in U.S. college sports. The NCAA’s May 2024 rules included women’s rugby and stated: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [4]
  • Because A review of studies of non-athletic transgender women found higher strength and muscle measures than in women female at birth after hormone treatment: “values remain above that observed in cisgender women, even after 36 months.” [5]
  • Because World Rugby links size and speed differences to injury: “When two opponents in a tackle are significantly different with respects to mass or speed, these risk factors increase significantly.” [6] The passage concerns head and neck injury risks.
  • Because Its review of testosterone reduction concluded that “safety and fairness cannot presently be assured for women competing against transwomen in contact rugby.” [7]
  • So Where hormone-based rules allowed these matchups, H.R.28 would prevent them in covered female competitions. This removes the collision hazard from those matchups.
  • So Safer conditions for an ordinary way to exercise serve [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury and danger.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Snopes (March 2025) states that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender, and that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. It reports that the school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence, that the board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players while several coaches spoke for continuing, and that North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, with their sports unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [8], [9], [10].

Evidence note: World Rugby's estimate models typical male mass against typical female mass. A 2024 athlete study recommends evaluating transgender women athletes as their own group rather than using cisgender men as proxies. The hormone review did not report activity levels of the groups compared. Sources: [6], [11], [5].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [12], [13].

points.title: It protects girls’ opportunities to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects girls’ opportunities to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.

  • Because Limited places can mean lost participation. ABC7 reported that Taylor Starling was moved to junior varsity when a transgender runner joined a seven-place varsity team, “causing Starling to miss a varsity cross-country meet.” [14] After a Title IX complaint she “was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet.” [14]
  • Because The bill reserves female competition for females at birth. It also conditions male practice on protecting each female’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • So It prevents that source of exclusion from female competition and practice. Where a girl has no other team place, that keeps her chance to exercise on a team open.
  • Because The federal health department explains that sports “participation is one way for youth to get the physical activity they need to be fit and healthy.” [15]
  • Because A U.S. study compared girls with boys during Title IX’s expansion of girls’ sports. It reported that the expansion “resulted in greater physical activity and improved weight and body mass.” [16]
  • Because CDC states that “regular physical activity prevents risk factors for various health conditions like heart disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes.” [17]
  • Because CDC also reports that active youth have “stronger bones and muscles.” [17] Its listed brain-health benefits include “reduced symptoms of depression.” [17]
  • So Keeping sports opportunities open protects a route to exercise and its physical and mental health benefits. Protecting that route serves [NAME]’s wish to protect health and avoid disease.
points.con_html:
Response The roster example does not show lost access to healthy exercise.

  • Because Starling “was bumped down to the JV team.” [14] JV means junior varsity.
  • Because The report adds that “she was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet. ML remains on the team as well.” [14]
  • So Starling retained access to school sports, and both runners ultimately participated on varsity. Losing varsity status for one meet does not establish reduced exercise or lost health benefits.
  • Because The health study concerns an expansion of participation: “Title IX caused a significant increase in girls’ sports participation.” [16]
  • So That research concerns girls added to sports, while the PRO’s example concerns a girl who stayed active. The evidence does not supply the step from displacement to less exercise. This response does not address a girl cut from a capped team with no other place to play.

points.title: It protects bodily privacy in female changing activities tied to team participation.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects bodily privacy in female changing activities tied to team participation.

  • Because The bill’s reach includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • So A changing activity designated for women or girls and made conditional on team participation falls within its female-only participation rule.
  • Because Unwanted shared undressing can damage a sense of security. Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines saying, “We did not give our consent to be exploited and exposed to a 6-foot-4 fully naked man.” [9] She added, “You allowed college women to be traumatized” [9].
  • So Applying the rule to those changing activities removes that route to unwanted shared undressing. Privacy in intimate settings supports feeling personally secure, which [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The bill’s text and the quoted account do not show that shared changing is a covered activity.

  • Because The bill limits its new definition of sex to “the purposes of this subsection” [1].
  • Because Its definition of athletic activities “includes, but is not limited to, all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Walberg quotes Gaines describing the exposure: “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” [9]
  • So That account does not establish that access depended on team participation or that the shared changing was itself a covered athletic activity. A room's connection to sports does not establish the condition on which the PRO's legal argument rests. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect As of January 14, 2025, H.R.28 would bar transgender girls and women from girls' and women's competitions at federally funded schools. It would make it unlawful for funded sports programs “to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1], defining sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1]. This would close options schools had then: many schools and athletic associations “have allowed equal participation for transgender athletes for years” [9].

points.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse, and trauma.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse, and trauma.

  • Because The bill sets a birth-sex rule but leaves the checking method open. Representative Hayes noted that it provides “neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” [18].
  • Because Idaho enacted an intrusive sex-check rule. The Ninth Circuit described it as allowing “intrusive medical procedures to verify her sex, including gynecological exams” [19].
  • Because The National Women's Law Center and Women's Sports Foundation warn that H.R.28 invites “invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [9] that “make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [9].
  • Because Such checks also threaten mental health. The court explained: “The psychological burden of these searches falls not only on transgender women like Lindsay but also on all women and girls who play female athletics.” [19]
  • Because Fear of checks threatens participation too. Representative Randall warned that intrusive questions and examinations would be “dissuading girls' participation in sports” [9].
  • So The new federal eligibility rule creates risks of bodily intrusion, abuse, and distress in an ordinary school activity. It also threatens the health benefits of exercise described in reason 3. Avoiding these dangers serves [NAME]'s aim to stay safe and healthy.
points.con_html:
Response Idaho's separate medical-testing rule does not establish that H.R.28 would expose girls to intrusive exams.

  • Because H.R.28 defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without ordering medical inspections. Its House manager described the intended method: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [9]
  • Because The Idaho court tied intrusive checks to that state's separate “sex dispute verification provision” [19]. It also reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [19]
  • So The PRO's own court source supplies a working alternative to intrusive exams under comparable restrictions. Idaho shows that a legislature can choose exams, but it does not show that schools under H.R.28 would choose them over records. The PRO’s claims of exam-related abuse and trauma depend on that step. This response does not address records-based inquiries, or fear and withdrawal caused by the possibility of challenges.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Idaho's statute included a separate sex-dispute verification process, which the Ninth Circuit described as allowing gynecological exams. The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [19], [1].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [20].

points.title: Public challenges to girls' sex expose them to harassment and threats of violence.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Public challenges to girls' sex expose them to harassment and threats of violence.

  • Because The Leadership Conference warns that H.R.28 “will invite scrutiny and harassment of any other student perceived by anyone as not conforming to sex stereotypes” [9].
  • Because This kind of accusation has already put a girl in danger. After a Utah school board member questioned a basketball player's sex, the board found that her post “created a substantial risk of harm” [21].
  • Because The girl was not transgender. The National Women's Law Center and Women's Sports Foundation report that the resulting threats required “police protection for her and her family” [9].
  • So Making birth sex a federal condition for playing gives these accusations a new role in decisions about who can play. Threats against girls who are not transgender and their families make this a safety concern in ordinary school sports, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Existing Title IX rules allowed separate sex-based teams. The Utah board treated the post as a breach of existing duties, including respecting student privacy and preventing harassment. H.R.28 creates no procedure for publicly disputing a student's sex. Sources: [22], [21].

points.title: The exclusion cuts off a route to exercise, mental health support, and health checkups.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The exclusion cuts off a route to exercise, mental health support, and health checkups.

  • Because The ban reaches recreational school sports as well as elite competition. As Representative Bonamici explained, “this bill applies to every student of every age in every sport the same way” [9].
  • Because Federal health guidance links youth sports with “Increased physical activity levels” [15] and physical activity with “Reduced risk of cancer and diabetes” [15].
  • Because A Colorado survey linked playing on three or more sports teams, versus none, to “reduced likelihood of depression” [23] among transgender students.
  • Because Sports also supply supportive relationships. The study cites research showing that “increased social support in adolescence, including that provided by team sports participation, protects against depression” [23].
  • Note The bill's conditional permission “to train or practice” [1] leaves the competition ban in place.
  • Because Boys' teams do not keep every excluded girl in sports. Surveyed transgender girls reported avoiding sports because they feared being “forced to play on a team or use a facility that does not align with their gender identity” [24].
  • Because Leaving sports also risks losing a reason to see a doctor. In a study of providers who care for transgender youth, one warned that patients who no longer need sports exams “may miss health issues and immunizations due to not coming in” [25].
  • So Closing access to competition removes a way to sustain exercise and supportive relationships. For students driven out of sports, it also puts sports-linked checkups at risk. Protecting physical and mental health gives [NAME] a reason to oppose these losses.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Colorado study measured the number of sports teams played and states that it cannot assess whether team participation directly reduces adverse mental-health outcomes. The missed-checkup statement is one provider's prediction, and the provider study notes that its prompt lacked precision because many bills do not ban participation outright. Sources: [23], [25].

points.title: Official rejection threatens mental health beyond students who lose a team place.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Official rejection threatens mental health beyond students who lose a team place.

  • Because Denying students a place in school athletics marks them as outsiders. The Leadership Conference describes this as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth” [9].
  • Because Medical researchers warn that these laws can “worsen the mental health of those who aren't directly targeted by these laws (e.g., trans youth who don't play sports)” [25].
  • Because The effects may reach teammates too. A suggested advocacy letter from the American Psychological Association warns that “excluding any subset of girls from sports can encourage divisiveness and compromise group cohesion, undermining the benefits all youth deserve from team sports” [26].
  • Because Supportive school relationships matter for health. CDC's research review describes school communities “lessening emotional distress, anxiety, and depression” [27].
  • So The law's rejection of some students threatens the supportive school ties that protect mental health, even without anyone leaving a sport. Protecting health in everyday school life gives [NAME] another reason to oppose it.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The APA divisiveness language appears in suggested advocacy text asking legislators to oppose a bill, and it cites an ACLU document. It reports no study of a sports eligibility rule. CDC lists other school supports, including student-led clubs, enforced antiharassment policies and caring student-teacher relationships. H.R.28 does not address those. Sources: [26], [27].

pages.description: H.R.28 would bar federally funded schools from allowing students who were born male — as defined by reproductive biology and genetics — to compete in sports programs designated for women or girls. It would make such participation illegal sex discrimination under Title IX.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law on January 14, 2025, H.R.28 would add a national eligibility rule to Title IX, the law against sex discrimination in federally funded education. It would make it unlawful for a funding recipient “to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] Sex would depend on “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] Its training and practice exception applies “as long as such training or practice does not deprive any female of corresponding opportunities or benefits.” [2]

points.title: It gives the United States an enforceable, lasting safeguard against injury risks from physical mismatches in women’s contact competition.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It gives the United States an enforceable, lasting safeguard against injury risks from physical mismatches in women’s contact competition.

  • Because Title IX lacked an express rule for transgender athletes: “Neither the statute nor the regulations currently address how Title IX applies to transgender athletes.” [3]
  • Because The NCAA’s May 2024 rules allowed transgender women to qualify for women’s rugby through a testosterone limit. The rules state, “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [4] The rugby row sets its blood testosterone limit at “<10 nmol/L” [4].
  • Because A 2021 review of studies in non-athletic transgender women found evidence of retained strength after hormone treatment: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5]
  • Because World Rugby explains how size and speed differences affect injury risk in tackles: “the discrepancy in mass and speed of direct opponents in tackles predicts neck forces, moments and head accelerations.” [6] It adds, “Since these factors contribute directly to injury risk, it is clear that large discrepancies create greater risks for smaller and slower players, particularly when size and speed exist in combination.” [6]
  • Because World Rugby’s review connects retained advantages after hormone treatment to that contact risk: “The lowering of testosterone removes only a small proportion of the documented biological differences, with large, retained advantages in these physiological attributes, with the safety and performance implications described previously.” [6]
  • So In covered women’s rugby, the bill would exclude competitors who went through male puberty and retain those advantages. That removes this source of competition risk rather than relying on a testosterone limit to remove it.
  • Because Title IX already provides ways to enforce the new duty: “Title IX is primarily enforced in two ways: through private litigation in federal court and by federal agencies that distribute funding to education programs.” [3]
  • So Making that participation an express Title IX violation gives federal agencies and affected students a legal basis to demand compliance across covered schools, including where state rules permit it.
  • So Writing the eligibility test into the law also prevents a future administration from reversing that duty simply by changing an agency’s interpretation of Title IX.
  • Note The January 2025 ruling had already removed the 2024 Title IX regulation: “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [3] Removing that regulation had not enacted the bill’s express national eligibility duty.
  • So Enforceable, lasting protection against this physical risk strengthens the country’s ability to defend its citizens through federal institutions. That serves [NAME]’s wish for a strong U.S. state that protects citizens against threats.
points.con_html:
Response Making protection from rugby injuries a lasting federal duty does not establish the gain in societal security the PRO claims.

  • Because This value distinguishes society’s safety from personal safety: “Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety.” [7]
  • Because World Rugby’s injury argument concerns impacts on players’ bodies: “the discrepancy in mass and speed of direct opponents in tackles predicts neck forces, moments and head accelerations.” [6]
  • So That evidence addresses players’ safety. It does not show how the risk threatens the country’s security or stability.
  • Because The enforcement channels already exist: “Title IX is primarily enforced in two ways: through private litigation in federal court and by federal agencies that distribute funding to education programs.” [3]
  • So A new eligibility duty changes what those institutions enforce. Its national reach and protection from reversal by agency interpretation do not show that those institutions become better able to meet threats to society.
  • So The PRO needs a link from its sports protection to a safer, more stable country or a stronger state able to defend its citizens. Federal enforcement and a lasting rule do not supply that link.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: It gives Congress evidence to check the sports rule’s safeguards.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It gives Congress evidence to check the sports rule’s safeguards.

  • Because The bill ties a federal study to the training and practice exception: “The Comptroller General shall carry out a study to determine the meaning of the phrase `any other benefit' as used in subsection (d)(4)” [1]. Those are benefits the exception must preserve.
  • Because The study must examine harms and lost benefits, including “deprivation of the benefit of an environment free of hostility based on sexual assault or harassment” [1].
  • Because The bill requires the study’s results to reach both congressional education committees in “a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So Congress would receive a required review of harms and benefits relevant to the rule’s safeguards. This gives lawmakers information to check whether those safeguards protect girls and where further action is needed.
  • So A state better equipped to find gaps in its protections is better equipped to defend citizens. That gives [NAME] a separate reason to favor the bill’s required review.
points.con_html:
Response Information about sports benefits does not supply the missing link to the state’s ability to protect society.

  • Because The study’s assigned purpose is “to determine the meaning of the phrase `any other benefit' as used in subsection (d)(4)” [1], which sets the training and practice exception.
  • Because Its subject is “benefits to women or girls of participating in single sex sports that would be lost by allowing males to participate.” [1]
  • Because The bill sends the results to Congress: “the Comptroller General shall submit to the Committee on Education and the Workforce of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions of the Senate a report that contains the results of such study.” [1]
  • So These provisions explain what lawmakers would learn about the benefits the exception must preserve. They do not explain how that knowledge improves the country’s security or stability or its ability to meet threats to society.
  • So Calling Congress better equipped to find gaps in sports protections repeats the first point’s unsupported step. The PRO still needs to show why better oversight of those protections serves societal security.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect H.R.28 would make allowing transgender girls and women classified as male at birth into girls’ and women’s competition a federal Title IX violation. Title IX “prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education programs.” [3] The bill bars recipients of federal aid from allowing “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It defines sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] This changes the January 14, 2025 baseline: “Many State schools and athletic associations across the country have allowed equal participation for transgender athletes for years” [10]. That baseline already reflects the loss of the 2024 Title IX regulations: “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [3]

points.title: The birth-sex rule creates pressure for invasive checks that expose girls to sexual abuse.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The birth-sex rule creates pressure for invasive checks that expose girls to sexual abuse.

  • Because Schools must meet the new rule without a clear method for checking sex. Representative Hayes explains: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [11]
  • Because Another birth-sex sports ban shows the enforcement risk. In 2024, a federal appeals court described Idaho’s law as allowing sex challenges and checks “including gynecological exams.” [12]
  • Because The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that checks under H.R.28 “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [10]. They identify the danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [10].
  • Note The floor manager proposes checking “a person's birth certificate.” [10] The bill gives that document no final say. Its test remains “reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] His assurance does not prevent schools from adopting invasive checks.
  • So Creating an abuse risk in schools weakens the state’s protection of its citizens. [NAME]’s commitment to a strong state that can defend them gives a reason to oppose this rule.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s evidence does not show that H.R.28 would push schools toward invasive checks and increase exposure to sexual abuse.

  • Because Idaho added a specific rule for medical checks: “A dispute regarding a student’s sex shall be resolved by the school or institution by requesting that the student provide a health examination and consent form or other statement signed by the student’s personal health care provider that shall verify the student’s biological sex.” [12]
  • Because The same court reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [12] It also said that, among the other 24 states with restrictions, “none has authorized a similar sex verification process.” [12]
  • Because H.R.28 defines sex through “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without adding Idaho’s procedure for medical checks. Its floor manager proposed using records: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [10]
  • So Idaho’s added procedure explains the risk of invasive checks in that example. The wider comparison shows an established way to check sex through records. The PRO does not show why H.R.28’s definition or its failure to make birth certificates final would displace that approach. Its warning therefore does not establish the added pressure needed for its abuse claim.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and remanded both. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow States to maintain female sports teams defined by biological sex, and that they do not require an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules; it does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [13].

points.title: The rule invites public accusations that threaten students and their communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The rule invites public accusations that threaten students and their communities.

  • Because The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights coalition warns that H.R.28 “will invite scrutiny and harassment of any other student perceived by anyone as not conforming to sex stereotypes” [10]. The risk reaches girls whose bodies or appearance prompt suspicion, whether they are transgender or not.
  • Because Such accusations already threaten school safety. The Salt Lake Tribune reported: “A Utah high school student needs police protection after a state school board member publicly singled out and suggested the student was transgender — without evidence — inciting threats from her followers on social media.” [14]
  • Because Hostility aimed at a group can intimidate a whole community. The Justice Department explains this wider harm in discussing hate crimes: “They represent an attack not just on the individual victim, but on the victim's community.” [15]
  • So Extending birth-sex eligibility rules to federally funded schools nationwide creates more occasions for this intimidation. Protecting citizens and their communities from threats gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: The Salt Lake Tribune reports the same board member was reprimanded in fall 2021 after a post that led some followers to threaten violence, before Utah's 2022 ban. It also reports a "slew of accusations" from parents and others after the law passed. Sources: [14].

points.title: Exclusion cuts access to sports as a way to build safer communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Exclusion cuts access to sports as a way to build safer communities.

  • Because Ordering transgender students onto teams based on sex at birth drives some out of sport. A 2025 study summarizes earlier research: “policies requiring youth to play on teams with their assigned sex, dissuade youth from participating” [16].
  • Because The loss also reaches girls born with variations in sex traits, often called intersex variations. The women’s sports organizations report: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [10]
  • Note The conditional practice exception permits “males to train or practice” [1]. It guarantees no place in practice and leaves the competition ban intact.
  • So Where schools now include them, the bill cuts off a route into sport for students it excludes or deters.
  • Because Sports also provide a setting linked to less use of illegal drugs. A review of 17 studies that followed young people over time reports: “Sport participation was associated with reduced illicit drug use during adolescence.” [17]
  • Because The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) describes organized sports as a tool for violence prevention: “Research shows that organized sport participation can reduce youth violence” [18].
  • Because School sports build community ties. The civil rights coalition explains that “School athletics are very often the centerpiece of communities across the country” [10] and that exclusion means “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10] HHS links sports with “Improved teamwork, social skills, and social responsibility” [19].
  • Because Community ties are associated with public safety. The Surgeon General links stronger community ties with “lower levels of community violence” [20].
  • So Exclusion closes a route to cooperation, community ties, less illegal drug use and, on HHS’s account, violence prevention. Preserving those forms of protection helps the United States protect its people. That serves [NAME]’s goal of a secure, stable country.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s research does not establish that changed eligibility would reduce violence prevention or community safety.

  • Because HHS cites “McMahon S, Belur J. Sports-based Programmes and Reducing Youth Violence and Crime.” [18] That review states: “None of the evaluations present robust enough evidence to directly establish causal links between interventions and outcomes.” [21] It reports some correlational evidence, not proof of cause.
  • Because A separate review of studies on youth crime concludes that “in general, sports involvement is not reliably related to more or less juvenile delinquency” [22]. HHS itself says: “Coaching, program design, and funding affect these outcomes” [18].
  • So Fewer sports places cannot simply stand for lost crime prevention. The PRO has not linked the affected programs to the features that provide that protection.
  • Because The Surgeon General’s discussion of lower crime concerns residents’ “willingness to act” [20] for community members.
  • So Losing a school sports tie and losing neighborhood trust are different outcomes, and the PRO does not connect them. This response does not address the PRO’s drug-use route.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The values paper cited in this exchange states: "Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety." The fixed value statements for this value include having a strong state that can defend its citizens. Sources: [7].

Evidence note: The mental-health study compared any team participation with none, and its authors say they could not deduce causal relationships and that depression can make participation harder. HHS introduces its mental-health and disease findings with "is associated with". The suicide figure describes existing risk among transgender and questioning students. HHS associates youth sports with reduced suicide risk and physical activity with reduced cancer and diabetes risk, and one study found lower depressive and anxiety symptoms among team athletes. CDC reports that about 26% of transgender and questioning students attempted suicide in the past year. Sources: [16], [19], [23].

Evidence note: The Surgeon General's advisory reports that people in neighborhoods connected to community institutions prepare for and recover from natural hazards more quickly. That passage does not address school sports. Sources: [20].

to follow their family's customs or the customs of a religion

pages.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
pages.description: H.R.28 would bar federally funded schools from allowing students who were born male — as defined by reproductive biology and genetics — to compete in sports programs designated for women or girls. It would make such participation illegal sex discrimination under Title IX.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on January 14, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If effective on January 14, 2025, H.R.28 would make male participation in female competition a Title IX violation for education programs receiving federal aid. It would prohibit permitting “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It would base sex solely on “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] Male training or practice would remain allowed when it “does not deprive any female of corresponding opportunities or benefits.” [2]

points.title: It applies a particular inherited Christian understanding of sex in school sports.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It applies a particular inherited Christian understanding of sex in school sports.

  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention affirmed in 2014 that “gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [3].
  • Because The bill uses that distinction for female sports eligibility: “sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]
  • So The bill makes a public sports rule follow the understanding of sex [NAME] wants to maintain.
  • Because The same faith statement says, “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [4].
  • Because The Family Research Council tells Christian parents to teach that “God created each of us either male or female” [5].
  • So Using birth sex for sports eligibility makes that public practice follow the male-and-female understanding parents are instructed to transmit. The bill does not regulate classroom teaching; the claimed connection is consistency between the sports rule and that particular inherited belief.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill's definition of sex applies "for the purposes of this subsection". It does not regulate what schools teach about gender identity. Sources: [1].

points.title: It preserves the established practice of separate female competition.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It preserves the established practice of separate female competition.

  • Because Separate school sports have a long legal history: “Long-standing Title IX regulations permit separation of the sexes in school sports programs provided schools offer equal athletic opportunities.” [6]
  • Because The Southern Baptist Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission identifies the cultural practice it wants to preserve: “Maintaining separate categories for males and females is essential to preserve the integrity and essence of women’s sports.” [7]
  • So Reserving female competition and its titles for female athletes preserves this form of women’s sports. [NAME]’s wish to honor cultural practices supports keeping it.
  • Note The January court ruling did not create the bill’s national requirement. CRS reports that “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [6] That removed the 2024 regulations; the longstanding sports rule quoted above permitted separate teams. H.R.28 would add an express requirement to exclude male competitors from female sports.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: NCAA policy from 2011 allowed transgender athletes in sex-separated sports subject to hormone-therapy conditions. On the comparison date the NCAA regulated eligibility sport by sport, with women's teams retained. Sources: [8], [6].

points.title: It gives families a way to carry out their traditional duty to protect women and girls.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It gives families a way to carry out their traditional duty to protect women and girls.

  • Because The Southern Baptist faith statement assigns the husband a protective role: “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.” [4]
  • Because Its Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission applies Christian duty to sports opportunities: “Christians should uphold biological reality, protect women’s opportunities, and preserve the sanctity of women’s sports by supporting such bans.” [7]
  • Because A 2021 review studied hormone treatment in transgender women who were not athletes. After one to three years of treatment, it found evidence of a lasting strength advantage over women born female: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [9]
  • Because The bill reserves female competition for female athletes and allows male practice only while protecting each female’s “roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So The bill protects female places and awards from going to male competitors and removes the risk of facing those competitors’ lasting strength advantages in female competition. Supporting this protection for daughters puts the inherited family duty into practice, giving [NAME] a reason grounded in Tradition to favor it.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s strength evidence is contested, so it does not establish the lasting strength advantage it says the bill would keep out of female competition.

  • Because The 2021 review studied hormone treatment to match gender identity, called GAHT, in “non-athletic transgender women” [9]. It limits its reach: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [9]
  • Because A 2026 review compares transgender women after hormone treatment with women whose gender identity matches their birth sex, called cisgender women. It reports: “While transgender women exhibited higher lean mass than cisgender women, their physical fitness was comparable.” [10] It concludes: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” [10] The July correction removed three studies, added one and states: “The main conclusions and key messages remain unchanged.” [11]
  • So The evidence does not establish the claimed lasting strength advantage in female competition, although its low certainty means it does not rule one out. This response does not address the PRO’s reason concerning places and awards, which rests on the duty its tradition states rather than on this evidence.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. Those intervals cross zero, with certainty rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are body-composition and fitness averages; the packet text reports no absolute mass, speed, collision or injury result by sport. Only the abstract and correction notice are in the packet, so its full methods were not verified. It postdates the comparison date but falls within the evidence cutoff. Sources: [10], [11].
points.retirement_reason: Protecting daughters' safety and opportunities is the substantive benefit. Calling it a father's religious duty does not independently establish a particular traditional practice.

points.title: It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.

  • Because Southern Baptists defend “the privacy concerns women rightly have about sharing sleeping quarters and intimate facilities with members of the opposite sex” [12].
  • Because Competition can bring access to changing facilities. The NCAA’s 2024 women’s swimming manual provides “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. It ties athlete access to credentials: “Team staff will receive numbered wristbands and student-athletes will receive labeled credentials. No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13]
  • Because Such access has been reported. Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines saying, “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” [14]
  • Because The bill covers activities beyond the contest itself, including “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • So A male athlete excluded from female competition cannot gain access to its private team activities through a place as a female competitor. Removing that route to shared intimate facilities supports the religious custom of privacy between the sexes that [NAME] wants to uphold.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that a female competition place itself grants shared intimate access, or that the bill covers those facilities.

  • Because The swimming manual describes “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. That passage does not identify which users may use which room or say those rooms are shared across sexes.
  • Because Its credential rule says, “No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13] This makes identification necessary for venue entry. It does not make a competition credential permission to change or shower with women.
  • Because The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Applying that clause to the claimed intimate access requires evidence that the access is a benefit conditional on team participation. The manual does not establish that condition for sharing intimate facilities with women.
  • So The PRO’s legal route to these facilities is not established. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.28?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect At covered schools receiving federal money, H.R.28 would make it unlawful “to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] It defines sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] This would end participation that some schools allowed on January 14, 2025: that day's debate recorded, “Many State schools and athletic associations across the country have allowed equal participation for transgender athletes for years” [14].

points.title: Barring children from their existing girls' competitions removes a shared way to pass on Christian virtues.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Barring children from their existing girls' competitions removes a shared way to pass on Christian virtues.

  • Because The rule also reaches activities reserved for team participants: “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Christian teaching values sports for building good habits, including self-control: “the virtues of temperance, humility, courage, patience can be fostered” [15].
  • Because This practice also has an American Christian ministry tradition: Upward Sports describes competition as “working together toward excellence with Christ-like love.” [16]
  • Because School teams provide these shared relationships: “Teams provide a place for kids to make friends and build relationships.” [14]
  • So Barring a child from the girls' games they already play removes shared competition with that team, a chance to practice these virtues together.
  • Because Seeking transgender children's good is part of the Southern Baptist Convention's teaching: “we love our transgender neighbors, seek their good always” [3]. The same resolution affirms that “gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [3], so this duty of care does not itself endorse girls' team placement.
  • Because The National Women's Law Center and Women's Sports Foundation warn that exclusion would “harm these students, who because of stigma and discrimination are already especially vulnerable to isolation and decreased academic performance” [14].
  • Because Uncertainty about the bill's definition of sex also threatens girls born with variations in sex traits, called intersex variations: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [14].
  • Because That warning concerns lost opportunities: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [14]
  • Because Christian teaching includes these children: “All persons are created in God’s image and are made to glorify Him” [3].
  • So Preserving this shared way to teach virtues, and following the inherited duty to care for these children, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose taking away their existing team opportunities.
  • Note Permission for “males to train or practice” [1] does not restore playing in girls' games with the team.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO has not shown that keeping these particular girls' team places preserves the Christian practice of forming and caring for children.

  • Because The Baptist resolution it cites says to “affirm God’s good design that gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” [3].
  • Because The U.S. bishops' education and marriage committee chairmen applied that teaching to school sports in 2021. They said students whose gender identity differs from their sex should have athletic opportunities “in co-educational activities or, where sexes are separated, in accord with their given sex.” [17]
  • Because They paired that rule with care for those children: “Harassment or unjust discrimination against them in this regard is unequivocally immoral.” [17]
  • So These teachings make sex-based eligibility part of Christian care in sport. Showing that sport and friendship help teach virtues does not show that preserving a placement contrary to that rule carries on the practice these teachings describe. This response does not address girls with intersex variations whose eligibility is uncertain.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill bars "a person whose sex is male" and does not name intersex variations. The letter warning about intersex girls gives no rule or example showing which variations would be classified as male. Sources: [1], [14].
points.retirement_reason: General virtue formation and care through school teams are not shown to continue an inherited Christian practice; the religious ministry example does not establish that link for the covered teams.

points.title: The bill takes a decision about children's upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill takes a decision about children's upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.

  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention teaches that “parents are the primary stewards of and decision-makers for their children, rather than teachers, doctors, or the state” [18].
  • Because Catholic teaching protects work that smaller groups can do themselves; it calls it an injustice to “assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.” [19]
  • Because Sports rules are already part of local responsibility: “Currently, schools, parents, and communities manage youth sports leagues and write rules about who can participate in different sports at different levels.” [14]
  • Because Existing individual reviews already weigh safety and fairness. The Congressional Research Service describes Illinois's 2024–25 rules as “requiring approval to participate based on consideration of individual circumstances” [6] and considering whether “allowing eligibility would be inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • Because H.R.28 would remove that choice at covered schools. As Representative Norcross explained, “It inflicts blanket bans without the ability of states, local governments, schools, and parents to make reasonable exceptions.” [20]
  • So Even when parents and a willing school approve a child's participation after individual review, the federal rule would bar girls' competition if it classifies that child as male. Preserving the family and local roles taught by [NAME]'s tradition gives a reason to oppose that loss of authority.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO has not shown that the particular sports exception removed belongs to the family and local duties its religious sources protect.

  • Because The cited Baptist resolution places parents' decisions “under the authority of God, recognizing that they will be held responsible for their choices” [18].
  • Because The Southern Baptist Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission explains: “The duty of parental authority is not the right to teach children whatever they desire. Rather, it is normed by what is good, true, and righteous.” [21]
  • Because That same body addressed this sports decision on January 13, 2025: “Schools that allow biological males to participate in female sports programs are discriminating against biological females.” [22]
  • So In this account, parental and school approval does not turn that eligibility exception into an exercise of Christian care or rightful parental teaching. The PRO cannot infer that religious authority protects the exception simply because parents and a school want it.
  • Because The Catholic principle of leaving work to smaller groups also serves duties beyond those groups. The PRO's source says, “To ensure the common good, the government of each country has the specific duty to harmonize the different sectoral interests with the requirements of justice” [19].
  • Because Illinois's 2024–25 policy made eligibility a decision for the statewide sports association: “IHSA will make final rulings on student participation.” [23] Its review considered whether eligibility would be “inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • So Showing that a lower body can run a review does not establish that its eligibility standard meets the religious account of justice. The PRO has not shown that allowing this exception is a duty the cited traditions reserve to families or local groups. Its claim of lost religious authority therefore lacks the needed link.

points.title: Sex-eligibility disputes can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Sex-eligibility disputes can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.

  • Because Schools would have to apply the bill's definition of sex, but it sets no method for checking disputed eligibility: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [24]
  • Because The women's sports organizations warn that resulting checks “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [14].
  • Because Intimate questioning has occurred under a comparable state ban. The National Women's Law Center reports that a Florida investigation included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25]
  • Because Catholic teaching connects children's privacy to moral upbringing: “Respect for privacy must be considered in close connection with decency and modesty” [26].
  • So Applying the rule in schools that now allow participation would require them to settle sex-eligibility disputes. The Florida account documents intimate questioning, and the organizations also warn of invasive checks. For [NAME], keeping the particular religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy supplies the Tradition connection; general safety and dignity are separate justifications.
points.con_html:
Response The floor manager identifies a records-based route, limiting the argument about bodily examinations.

  • Because The bill adds a violation of the federal education law, Title IX, for “a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] and defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1]. Its text sets no examination procedure.
  • Because The floor manager described a records-based way to apply the bill: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [14]
  • Because The Florida source reports a state investigation that included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25] That describes questioning, not a bodily examination.
  • So The floor manager’s records-based account bears on the proposed route from this rule to bodily examinations. It does not answer the documented risk of intimate questioning, or establish that the religious modesty concern disappears. This is a limited response to the examination branch only.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Education Department's civil-rights manual limits release of documents that would cause an unwarranted invasion of privacy. Illinois's association policy kept eligibility documents confidential unless the student or parents asked otherwise. The Utah board treated the public post as a breach of rules requiring members to respect student privacy. Sources: [27], [23], [28].
